reading.rtitle: Two Kids, One Envelope -- what college really costs around here
paras: Every fall, families in this area open the same envelope and feel the same thing. The number on the page is called the cost of attendance, and at a private university it now sits close to eighty thousand dollars a year. That figure is not only tuition. It includes room and board, campus fees, books, and an estimate of what a student will spend on a bus. Counselors even have a name for the moment the envelope is opened: sticker shock. What they will tell you, and what is true, is that almost nobody pays the number printed on the page. The problem is that families make big decisions in the ten minutes before they learn that.

The first thing that moves the number is geography. A public university charges one price to students whose families live and pay taxes in the state, and a much higher price to everybody else. In Virginia this year, an in-state student pays about fifteen thousand dollars in tuition; the same seat costs a student from another state more than fifty. Residency is not a matter of opinion. States check driver's licenses, tax returns and how long the family has actually been there. For a household that has just arrived from another country, this single line is the most expensive one in the whole letter, and it is worth asking about two years early.

The second thing that moves the number is the aid office. Financial aid is money the university takes off the price after it looks at what a family earns and owns. A scholarship is money a student is given for grades, for a sport, or for a major the department is trying to fill. The two are counted together, and both start with a form the family files in the fall of the student's senior year. Filing late is the most common and the most expensive mistake in this whole process, because some of the money simply runs out. A student who applies to a school in December and files that form in March is not applying to the same school.

So what are families around here actually doing? Some are taking out a loan, which is still the most common answer and the one that follows a household for twenty years. Some are sending a student to a community college for two years and transferring after that, which saves more than any scholarship most students will ever win. A few are choosing a cheap dorm over a famous name. And a growing number are taking a gap year, working and saving and starting when they are ready. The families who stay on track are not the ones with the most money. They are the ones who started asking these questions long before the first form was due.
reading.source: Local paper -- education section, Washington, DC

listenings.text: So people ask me what that year was actually like, and honestly, the calendar was the hard part. The first deadline was November first, and I mean the whole file: the essay, the recommendations, all of it. We drove to four campuses in one week in October, which I would not do again. Two of them she loved. At one of them, you know, we walked in and she said, I do not want to be here, and we turned around after twenty minutes. Our real mistake was the financial aid form. We filed it in February, and by February the money at her first-choice school was already gone. So she got in, she got a small scholarship, and the number at the bottom of that letter was still forty-one thousand dollars a year. She is in-state now, at a school she never visited, and she is happy. That is the part nobody tells you.

Hello, this is a recorded message from the front office at Wilson High School, with information for the families of our seniors. Our senior parent night will be held on Thursday, October fourteenth, at seven p.m., in the main auditorium, and it is going to run about ninety minutes. A counselor from the district will walk you through the whole calendar: application deadlines, the financial aid form, and what to expect from the cost letters that arrive in the spring. Please bring your student's course list and last year's tax return, because the aid workshop in the second half is hands-on. Coffee is served from six thirty. If your student is applying to more than five schools, we do recommend the extra session on Saturday morning. Questions about deadlines go to Ms. Ortiz, counseling at Wilson dot edu. Thank you, and we will see you on the fourteenth.

Everybody has an opinion about the gap year, and I have changed mine twice. The argument against it is simple: you lose momentum. A kid who stops after high school sometimes never starts again, and there is real money in that, because a year out is a year of tuition you end up paying later, at a higher price. I have seen it happen. On the other side, and this is where I have landed, half the students I work with are perfectly on track on paper and have absolutely no idea why they are there. They are going to spend forty thousand dollars a year finding out. So my position is this. Take the year, but make it a real year: work, save, do something that scares you a little. And apply before you go, so the seat is waiting for you when you come back. That last part is the whole trick.
